title: Google DeepMind picks 16 climate-AI projects across Asia-Pacific for inaugural 'AI for the Planet' accelerator
subtitle: The three-month program opens with an in-person bootcamp in Singapore and gives startups access to Google's environmental models — AnthroKrishi, ForestCast, AlphaEarth Foundations, SpeciesNet, and Perch.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind announced on September 7 the first cohort of its 'AI for the Planet' accelerator — 16 startups, nonprofits, and research teams from Australia, India, Indonesia, Japan, New Zealand, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand, selected from an APAC-wide open call. The program opened this week with a hands-on bootcamp in Singapore and runs three months, followed by virtual mentorship through December and a demo day. Support is equity-free, with cloud credits for eligible projects and no disclosed cash grants.

The specific technical hook is access to Google's stack of environment-focused models: AnthroKrishi for agriculture, ForestCast for forest-carbon and deforestation, AlphaEarth Foundations for Earth-observation embeddings, SpeciesNet for wildlife identification, and Perch for bioacoustic analysis of animal calls. Participants also get direct mentorship from DeepMind researchers. Four of the 16 selected teams are Indian, matching the size of India's contribution to Google's open-source and Kaggle activity over the last year.

This is the first DeepMind accelerator run entirely outside the US and UK, and it lands the same week that Google's Q2 AI-momentum narrative was reset by Gemini 3.8 Flash's coding lead. Climate-AI is a low-margin category — the models rarely earn API revenue at frontier-model rates — so a program like this is best read as ecosystem-and-standards building rather than a direct commercial bet. It matters more if the models participants build become the default that governments and NGOs cite when they procure environmental analytics, than if any single startup exits.

For learners: 'AI for good' programs are often dismissed as marketing, but the ones that ship durable tools tend to have three ingredients this cohort has — real production models rather than sandboxes, region-specific problem framing rather than a global template, and mentorship from the researchers who built the models. If you want to see whether the pattern is real, watch the demo day in December: count how many of the 16 projects still have working demos, and how many of those are actually deployed with a partner organization.
